Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in the United States, emphasizing public health and moral imperatives.
Model Response:

Title: A Renewed Call for National Prohibition: Protecting Public Health and Morality

Introduction
Calls to reinstitute the prohibition of alcohol in the United States might seem anachronistic in an era shaped by personal choice and free markets. Yet, with the costs of alcohol-related harm rising and moral imperatives beckoning for a societal shift, the possibility of reestablishing a national prohibition gains renewed legitimacy. Many of the same arguments that informed the original Prohibition movement in the early 20th century — such as protecting families, reducing crime, and safeguarding public health — still resonate today. By examining health statistics, economic costs, and social consequences, we can see why banning the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages could be a bold and beneficial course for the modern era.

  1. Addressing the Public Health Crisis
    Alcohol is directly linked to a multitude of health problems. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), excessive drinking contributes to death and permanent health issues for countless Americans each year. Alcohol-related liver disease, cardiovascular problems, and certain types of cancers are prevalent in communities where heavy drinking is normalized or even celebrated. Furthermore, alcohol impairs judgment and can induce risky behavior, leading to accidents and injuries.
    • Reduction in Alcohol-Related Deaths: A strict prohibition could significantly reduce fatalities from driving under the influence, liver cirrhosis, and alcohol poisoning. Even a modest decrease in alcohol-related deaths would spare thousands of families the heartbreak and financial burdens that follow in the wake of personal tragedy.
    • Improved Overall Well-Being: A prohibition would help curb binge drinking, which has been shown to contribute to chronic diseases. If alcohol is no longer legally available, the widespread culture of indulgence could slowly shift toward healthier choices, leading to better-quality lifestyles.

  2. Alleviating Economic Strains
    Critics often argue that banning alcohol would harm various industries — from breweries to bars to restaurants. While certain economic sectors would be affected, it is equally valid to scrutinize the tremendous societal cost of alcohol consumption and ask whether those burdens are acceptable.
    • Decreased Healthcare Expenditures: Alcohol misuse strains resources through emergency room visits, rehabilitation programs, and ongoing treatments for alcohol-related illnesses. With a prohibition, demand for these services would, in theory, decline, easing the burden on the healthcare system.
    • Productivity Gains: Excessive drinking impairs workplace performance, leading to absenteeism and lost productivity, which ultimately impacts the economy at large. A national ban would help minimize these losses by reducing alcohol’s availability, thereby fostering a more reliable and productive labor force in many sectors.

  3. Fostering Social and Familial Stability
    One of the primary arguments for Prohibition a century ago was social betterment — particularly the notion of strengthening families and communities. Alcohol can contribute to family conflict, domestic abuse, and neglect.
    • Reduced Domestic Violence: Although eliminating alcohol does not guarantee elimination of abuse in every household, the association between heavily intoxicated individuals and domestic violence is well-documented. The link between high alcohol usage and aggression underscores the moral obligation to intervene.
    • Better Parenting and Child Welfare: The negative effects of growing up in a household where one or both parents suffer from alcohol misuse can last a lifetime. By lowering access to alcohol, the number of children exposed to volatile, alcohol-fueled environments would likely decline, improving their developmental outcomes and overall well-being.

  4. Moral Imperatives and Community Values
    Beyond the tangible costs to health and safety, the proliferation of alcohol consumption raises moral and ethical concerns. Alcohol has often been associated with promiscuity, addictive behavior, and criminal activities. In communities that prioritize living free from dependence on harmful substances, the availability and normalization of alcohol pose a moral challenge.
    • Encouraging Temperance and Self-Control: A society that esteems moderation sacrifices that principle when it provides open access to a substance that many find difficult to regulate. By contrast, a prohibition would reinforce a cultural commitment to self-discipline and self-improvement.
    • Reinvigorating Moral Responsibility: Members of society, from local community leaders to national officials, would be compelled to re-emphasize sober living and healthy recreation as cornerstones of civic virtue. This shared value system could unite local communities, churches, and civic organizations in a renewed call for wholesome, spirit-free gatherings.

  5. Learning from Historical Precedent
    Critics rightly point to the issues that arose under the 18th Amendment and the era of speakeasies and bootlegging. Yet modernizing prohibition does not mean duplicating the methods of the early 20th century. In our present context, more sophisticated means of law enforcement, public education, community outreach, and substance abuse treatment could be deployed.
    • Focus on Rehabilitation Services: Instead of targeting users with harsh penalties, a contemporary prohibition could focus more robustly on treatment, recognizing that addiction is a pervasive medical and social condition.
    • Advanced Enforcement and Regulation: Today’s technology — such as better surveillance systems, data analytics, and improved border control methods — would help mitigate the black market problems that plagued the initial Prohibition era. Careful structuring of laws and penalties, alongside community-based programs, could drastically reduce illicit trade.

Conclusion
The reintroduction of a national prohibition on alcohol represents a monumental shift, one that inevitably faces challenges from cultural norms, industry interests, and individual freedoms. However, the stakes are undeniably high. At the heart of this proposal lies the desire to protect public health, safeguard families, and reinforce moral imperatives that oppose substance abuse. As healthcare costs continue to skyrocket and as families grapple with the tragic outcomes of alcohol-related harm, revisiting prohibition stands out as a bold but potentially transformative solution. If enacted thoughtfully and enforced through modernized approaches, a new era of prohibition could foster safer, more stable communities and offer tangible benefits to the nation’s collective well-being.

Question:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for reinstating a nationwide alcohol prohibition policy in the United States, focusing on its expected positive impact on public health, crime reduction, and social wellbeing.
Model Response:

Below is an overview of the main arguments often cited by proponents of strict liquor control or prohibition, focusing on the positive outcomes they hope prohibition would achieve for public health, crime reduction, and social wellbeing. While these points lay out potential benefits, it is worth noting that many of these arguments are highly debated, and historical attempts at prohibition have illustrated significant complexities and unintended consequences.

  1. Potential Public Health Advantages • Lower alcohol-related disease and mortality: By restricting or eliminating the availability of alcohol, proponents argue there would be fewer cases of alcohol-related illnesses, such as cirrhosis of the liver, certain cancers, and other chronic conditions. They also point to reduced alcohol consumption as a way to reduce overall healthcare costs.
    • Reduction in accidents and injuries: Alcohol is a factor in many motor vehicle accidents, workplace incidents, and interpersonal injuries. If legal, widespread access were curtailed, supporters believe the incidence of such accidents would drop, decreasing both the personal and societal expenses tied to emergency care and long-term rehabilitation.
    • Healthier youth development: Restricting alcohol could help prevent youths from acquiring alcohol as easily, decreasing early-age drinking. Early-age alcohol consumption is associated with higher risks of addiction and health complications later in life. By making it less accessible, supporters claim youth would avoid those risks.

  2. Crime Reduction Rationale • Less “alcohol-fueled” crime: Alcohol intoxication can contribute to violent behaviors such as assault, domestic violence, and other offenses. By reducing or removing access to alcohol, proponents expect a decline in these crimes, improving public safety.
    • Reduction in drunk driving offenses: Drunk driving is a major public-safety concern, with considerable social and economic costs. By theoretically eliminating legal alcohol sales and consumption, advocates of prohibition suggest the rate of alcohol-impaired driving and fatalities could be substantially reduced.
    • Lower burden on law enforcement: If alcohol use could be drastically reduced, law enforcement resources could be diverted away from policing alcohol-related incidents (e.g., bar fights, public intoxication). Prohibition supporters believe this would free up resources to address other forms of criminal activity.

  3. Social Wellbeing Arguments • Strengthening family stability: Alcohol misuse can disrupt family structures, causing neglect, abuse, or financial hardship. Proponents of prohibition suggest that disallowing alcohol entirely could reduce such stressors and enable more stable family environments.
    • Improving workplace productivity: Excessive alcohol use can lead to absenteeism, reduced job performance, or on-the-job accidents. Advocates argue that prohibition would help maintain a more productive workforce, benefiting the economy overall.
    • Promoting community cohesion: By removing a common source of social disorder (e.g., late-night disturbances, bar room brawls), prohibition supporters believe communities might enjoy a calmer social environment and feel safer, thereby fostering social trust and healthy neighborly relations.

  4. Underlying Philosophical or Moral Grounds • Morality and personal responsibility: Many prohibition advocates historically (and in modern times) see alcohol as intrinsically harmful to personal character and overall societal standards. They argue that banning it can facilitate a collective shift towards healthier, more responsible habits, in line with moral or religious values.
    • Cultural and generational change: Some proponents see prohibition as a tool to “reeducate” society away from dependence on alcohol, leading future generations to either avoid or significantly reduce their use of alcohol.

  5. Caveats and Ongoing Debates Even among those who highlight the potential benefits of strict liquor policies, there are important counterpoints and lessons learned from the historical era of Prohibition (1920–1933), which included:
    • A rise in unregulated or illegal markets, often accompanied by organized crime activity.
    • Potential human rights concerns and the costs of enforcing a widespread ban.
    • Social divisions and lack of public compliance if prohibition is not widely supported.
    • Economic losses from the closure of breweries, distilleries, bars, and related industries.

Summary
Supporters of nationwide alcohol prohibition underscore improved public health, crime reduction, and bolstered social wellbeing as their core justifications. They believe eliminating the legal sale and consumption of alcohol would markedly lower alcohol-related injuries and diseases, reduce crime associated with public intoxication and drunk driving, and foster more stable communities. However, the historical complexities and real-world outcomes of alcohol prohibition demonstrate that such policies also come with significant challenges—something policymakers must weigh when debating a modern nationwide ban.

By Imbibe-No-More Weekly Staff

In a world plagued by tormenting evils—like slouchy posture, mismatched socks, and that confounding phenomenon known as “daylight savings”—there remains one uniquely monstrous foe: the dreaded, soul-tempting existence of alcohol.

Yes, folks, it’s time we talk about resurrecting Prohibition, that triumphant historical era when the only twinkle in the average citizen’s eye was from the reflection of their homemade bathtub gin. Oh, wait…

But never mind the small, inconsequential details of history. This is about something far more noble: saving humanity from itself. Now, you might have heard that some misguided heretics, known collectively as “people who like a drink now and then,” are calling it an “overreach” to once again banish booze to the dark corners of a dusty cellar. But let’s dive in and see just how delightfully mistaken they are.

  1. The Self-Proclaimed “Connoisseurs” of Flavor
    Listen to any wine-swirler who claims the best way to explore the nuance of French oak casks is with a refined palate. What they truly mean is, “I haven’t discovered soup or sandwiches as a flavor experience, so I’m forced to rely on fermented grape juice.” If their sense of taste is really that refined, perhaps they should apply it elsewhere—like sampling the wide array of artisanal kale smoothies we can all enjoy during Prohibition. Because we all know there’s nothing more satisfying than the earthy goodness of liquefied leafy greens. Mmm, indeed.

  2. The Mysterious “Social Lubrication” Argument
    You’ve probably heard the old refrain: “A little booze helps me loosen up at parties!” Well, guess what—there’s another invention that loosens people up fabulously at get-togethers: conversation. Radical, right? Who would’ve thought that speaking coherent words to other humans could lead to forming a connection? But apparently, these social drinkers prefer the time-tested method of “grabbing a glass of liquid confidence, forgetting said gathering by midnight, and waking up thinking that lamp in the corner might have chased them around the living room.” Yes, that’s a real conversation-starter.

  3. The “Underage Problem” Hypocrites
    One of the loudest battle cries from those who oppose Prohibition is, “But think of the children!” Ah, yes—those poor, misguided youth who would never even consider a rebellious act if it weren’t for something being taboo. Let's be honest: kids are so rebellious they’d smuggle contraband crayons if you tried to prohibit them. Yet these naysayers would allow bars on every street corner, comforting themselves with the notion that age restrictions and ID checks miraculously prevent mischief. Because obviously, no teenager has ever found a, um… “creative” way to get around the rules. If we ban all the booze, it’s basically foolproof. Right?

  4. Economic Mayhem, You Say?
    Critics claim that banning alcohol threw the economy into turmoil the first time around. Apparently, the creation of the black market and the rise of covert cellar-swillers undermined legitimate businesses—shock and horror! But who’s to say we can’t learn from the past? With modern technology, we can introduce live-streamed speakeasy raids and maximum-security fermentation detectors! Think of all the new jobs in the Sober Security Sector. Market meltdown? More like market metamorphosis, baby! It’s practically a mania of virtuous progress.

  5. The Myth of “Personal Freedom”
    Finally, we come to the rallying cry of these so-called “liberty-loving” folks. “We should be free to choose what we consume!” they say, mistaking their misguided quest for personal autonomy with a right to get hammered on cheap beer they’ll regret in the morning. But is “freedom” really free if it runs the risk of someone belting out karaoke versions of old ’90s boy-band songs at 2 a.m.? No, dear reader, it most certainly is not. We must unite in the crusade to protect eardrums across the nation from tuneless serenades of yesteryear.

Conclusion:
In the grand tapestry of life, we all must pick a side. And truly, there’s no more gallant side than championing a complete ban on booze—except maybe banning processed sugar, or possibly oxygen if it eventually becomes too mainstream. Regardless, let us ignore the opposition’s flimsy arguments about “history” and “personal rights,” and instead embrace the sheer delight of moral purity. Here’s to a future where everyone’s water glasses are raised in unadulterated dryness and the only spirit lifting your soul is the knowledge that absolutely no one is out there, somewhere, responsibly enjoying a local craft brew.

So, to those who remain unconverted—those misguided individuals still celebrating birthdays with toast-worthy champagne and tepidly defending personal choice—our hearts go out to you. Truly, you must not understand the joy of lawfully mandated blandness. Raise your (non-alcoholic) cups in pity, dear supporters of dryness. The rest will come around eventually—once they’ve had enough watery herbal tea to see the error of their ways!

Ladies and gentlemen, fellow citizens:

I stand before you today to advocate for a cause that may seem, at first, to be a step back in time—a return to an era many now dismiss as drastic and misguided. Nevertheless, I urge you to hear my words and consider the greater good of our nation. I speak of the reintroduction of national prohibition on alcohol. This call is not made lightly; it stems from a profound concern for our collective welfare, our moral fiber, and our social harmony.

  1. Safeguarding Public Health
    First and foremost, reestablishing prohibition would serve as a powerful measure to protect public health. Excessive alcohol consumption contributes to a wide range of illnesses, from liver disease and cancers to heart problems and mental health disorders. It afflicts not only the individual but also the broader society. Families are torn apart by the physiological and psychological consequences of alcohol abuse, creating ripple effects that burden healthcare systems and strain social services. By removing alcohol from our shelves, we would dramatically reduce these public health challenges and secure a brighter, healthier future for generations to come.

  2. Reinforcing Strong, Thriving Communities
    Alcohol often serves as a catalyst for disruption and crime. Countless acts of violence, from domestic conflicts to public assaults, have been traced directly to excessive drinking. Neighborhoods suffer, as do our police forces, who must respond more frequently to alcohol-related emergencies. Under prohibition, crime rates linked to intoxication would drop, diminishing the strain on law enforcement and enabling communities to flourish. Children would grow up in safer homes, and the resources currently poured into combating alcohol-fueled offenses could be redirected toward education, public works, and community enrichment projects.

  3. Upholding Moral Standards
    There is no denying that a nation’s moral health is influenced by its collective spirit. Alcohol’s destructive capacity often undermines the very foundations of virtue—it clouds judgment, weakens resolve, and can lead individuals to abandon responsible and honorable behavior. By returning to prohibition, we would send a resounding message that we, as a nation, choose discipline over excess, resolve over surrender, and compassion for one another’s well-being over fleeting indulgence. A society committed to sobriety frees itself from dependency and reaffirms the values of responsibility, clarity of mind, and respect for one’s body, mind, and community.

  4. Fostering Economic Resilience
    Some might argue that alcohol is a pillar of economic prosperity given the revenue and jobs it generates. Yet, when we weigh those benefits against the staggering healthcare expenses and productivity losses due to alcohol-related ailments, the fiscal gains from the alcohol industry pale in comparison to the costs. Under prohibition, new opportunities would emerge in industries centered on non-alcoholic beverages, wellness, and healthy entertainment alternatives. We would reclaim resources desperately needed for social programs, educational initiatives, and infrastructure, leading to genuine, sustainable growth that does not come at the cost of public health or moral compromise.

  5. Celebrating American Strength and Unity
    Finally, we should reflect on who we are as a nation: courageous, innovative, and steadfast in our determination to protect each other and elevate our national character. Reinstating prohibition is not about denying pleasure; it is about lifting our country to a higher moral standard and a more unified sense of purpose. Throughout history, Americans have endured hardships and championed reforms for the greater good. We have confronted threats to our society head-on, time and time again. The challenge of curtailing alcohol may be daunting, but it is a sacrifice worth making—for our families, our communities, and the very soul of our nation.

In conclusion, I call upon you—fathers and mothers, business owners, educators, policymakers, and all individuals of conscience—to consider seriously the profound benefits that national prohibition could deliver. This is not a matter of restricting freedom; rather, it is a collective endeavor to safeguard our health, strengthen our moral foundations, support safer communities, and ensure a prosperous future for our children. Let us take this bold step together. Let us choose the higher path that unites us in dignity, responsibility, and care for one another.

Thank you, and may we move forward with courage and unity in establishing a society free from the destructive grasp of alcohol.

It is time to look back at the lessons of our past and boldly bring back national prohibition of alcohol.

We live in an age where the consequences of alcohol consumption are all too apparent. Every day, families are torn apart by the ravages of addiction. Hospitals overflow with victims of alcohol-related accidents and diseases. Our streets witness the tragic loss of life due to drunk driving. The statistics are staggering, but they cannot fully capture the pain and suffering inflicted upon countless individuals and communities.

Alcohol is not just a personal choice; it is a societal plague that affects us all. It is a substance that impairs judgment, fuels violence, and undermines the very fabric of our communities. How many more children must grow up in homes shattered by alcoholism? How many more promising lives must be cut short before we take decisive action?

Reintroducing prohibition is not about stripping away freedoms; it is about protecting our citizens and ensuring a brighter future for generations to come. It is about acknowledging that the costs of alcohol far outweigh any perceived benefits. The economic burden on our healthcare system, the loss of productivity, and the immeasurable human suffering demand that we act now.

Consider the moral imperative. As a society, we have a responsibility to uphold standards that promote the well-being of all. Alcohol blurs the lines of morality, leading to actions and decisions that one would not make when sober. It contributes to crime, domestic abuse, and a host of social ills that degrade our moral standards and compromise our collective integrity.

Some may argue that prohibition in the past was a failed experiment. But let us not forget that during the Prohibition era, alcohol consumption declined significantly, and so did alcohol-related health issues and deaths. The challenges faced then were due in part to inadequate enforcement and societal resistance rooted in a different time. Today, with modern resources, better education, and a more informed public, we can implement prohibition effectively.

We have successfully mobilized against other public health threats. We have imposed regulations to curb the dangers of tobacco, restricted harmful substances, and launched campaigns to promote healthier lifestyles. It's time we apply the same determination to alcohol—a substance that has caused untold damage for far too long.

Imagine a society where our emergency rooms are not flooded with alcohol poisoning cases, where our roads are safer, and where families are spared the heartache of losing loved ones to alcohol-related tragedies. Picture communities thriving without the shadow of bars on every corner, and youth growing up without the allure of alcohol as a rite of passage.

Bringing back prohibition is a bold move, but boldness is exactly what we need. It sends a clear message that we value the health, safety, and moral compass of our nation above the interests of an industry that profits from pain and addiction.

Let us rise to the occasion and make the courageous choice. Let us enact legislation that prioritizes the common good over individual indulgence. The time has come to take a stand—for our families, for our communities, and for the soul of our nation.

Together, we can forge a future that is healthier, safer, and morally steadfast. Let us bring back national prohibition of alcohol and pave the way for a better tomorrow.

Thank you.

Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in the United States, emphasizing public health and moral imperatives.
Model Response:

Reaffirming Temperance: The Case for a New National Prohibition on Alcohol in the United States

Introduction
For nearly a century, Americans have lived with the assumption that alcohol is an immutable fixture of social life. Yet the evidence against this assumption grows stronger each year. Alcohol remains one of the nation’s most pervasive public‑health threats, a catalyst for violence, an economic drain, and a driver of moral erosion. Reinstating a constitutional prohibition on the manufacture, sale, and consumption of alcoholic beverages is not a nostalgic call to relive the 1920s; it is a clear‑eyed recognition that the harms of alcohol dramatically outweigh its social conveniences. Viewed through the intertwined lenses of public health, economics, and moral responsibility, there is a compelling, urgent case for returning to a nationwide ban.

I. Public‑Health Imperatives

  1. A leading preventable killer
    • Alcohol contributes to roughly 140,000 deaths annually in the United States—more than opioids, more than all illicit drugs combined.
    • It is implicated in liver cirrhosis, at least seven types of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and compromised immune function.
    • Binge drinking among youth and adults has risen despite educational campaigns, illustrating voluntary moderation’s failure.

  2. Burden on the healthcare system
    • Alcohol‑related illnesses and injuries cost an estimated $249 billion each year, billions of which fall onto taxpayer‑funded Medicaid and Medicare.
    • Emergency departments spend scarce resources treating intoxication, alcohol‑induced assaults, and car‑crash victims. Prohibition would stem this flood at the source.

  3. Mental‑health consequences
    • Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant linked to major depressive disorder, anxiety, and suicide.
    • Family members of those with alcohol‑use disorder often develop secondary trauma, perpetuating cycles of mental illness.

II. Social and Economic Costs

  1. Workplace productivity losses
    • Up to 15 percent of U.S. employees report drinking on the job or coming to work hungover, costing employers tens of billions in lost productivity, absenteeism, and accidents.
    • Prohibition would remove a chief cause of occupational impairment and injury.

  2. Alcohol‑induced crime and violence
    • More than one in three violent crimes involves alcohol, including over half of all sexual assaults on college campuses.
    • Drunk‑driving crashes kill 10,000 Americans annually and injure hundreds of thousands more. Eliminating alcohol sales would drastically cut these tragedies at their root.

  3. Intergenerational harm
    • Children in households with heavy drinking are at higher risk for abuse, neglect, developmental delays, and substance use later in life.
    • Prenatal alcohol exposure remains the leading preventable cause of birth defects and intellectual disabilities.

III. Moral and Ethical Imperatives

  1. Upholding human dignity
    • A society that knowingly profits from a substance causing addiction and destruction violates the ethical principle of non‑maleficence—“first, do no harm.”
    • Government permits and taxes alcohol sales while simultaneously funding the fallout, an implicit moral contradiction.

  2. Protecting the vulnerable
    • Minors, recovering alcoholics, victims of drunk‑driving accidents, and unborn children lack meaningful protection in the current regulatory environment.
    • A national ban expresses collective solidarity with these vulnerable populations, prioritizing human well‑being over commercial interests.

  3. Reclaiming community cohesiveness
    • Alcohol often masks social bonds with chemical dependency; communities flourish when interaction relies on genuine connection, not intoxication.
    • Faith traditions, civic organizations, and families historically celebrated milestones without liquor—and can do so again.

IV. Answering Common Objections

  1. “Prohibition failed once; it will fail again.”
    • The prior experiment occurred amid weak federal enforcement, patchwork state cooperation, and technological limitations. Today’s surveillance tools, tracing methods, and interstate coordination vastly exceed 1920s capabilities.
    • Studies show that during the original Prohibition, cirrhosis deaths and public‑drunkenness arrests plummeted, proving that even imperfect enforcement saves lives.

  2. “Legalization prevents black markets.”
    • Black markets thrive on demand; reducing legal supply shrinks cultural normalization and overall consumption, thereby diminishing illicit profit potential.
    • With comprehensive enforcement and stiff penalties, modern technology can disrupt illegal networks far more effectively than a century ago.

  3. “Prohibition violates personal liberty.”
    • Civil society already restricts liberty where individual choices impose substantial harm on others—seat‑belt laws, speed limits, and restrictions on toxic substances are undisputed examples.
    • Alcohol’s externalities (injury to others, public spending, lost productivity) are so vast that limiting personal liberty in this domain is legally consistent and morally warranted.

  4. “Moderate drinking can be healthy.”
    • Claims regarding cardiovascular benefits of moderate alcohol intake have been largely debunked after controlling for confounding factors such as socioeconomic status and healthy lifestyle biases.
    • There is no safe level of alcohol consumption when net harms to society are considered.

V. Policy Blueprint for a Modern Prohibition

  1. Constitutional amendment
    • Introduce and ratify a 28th Amendment repealing the 21st Amendment, explicitly banning manufacture, distribution, and sale of alcohol nationwide.

  2. Public‑health transition period
    • Enact a three‑year phased reduction in commercial production to give farmers, distributors, and restaurants time to diversify into non‑alcoholic beverages and other commodities.
    • Allocate federal grants for breweries and distilleries to convert facilities toward producing kombucha, non‑alcoholic malt beverages, or biofuels.

  3. Robust enforcement and penalties
    • Establish a dedicated Alcohol Enforcement Bureau within the Department of Justice, leveraging data analytics, interstate task forces, and modern tracking to suppress bootlegging and online sales.
    • Severe but proportionate penalties targeting traffickers—fines, license revocations, and imprisonment—while focusing on treatment rather than incarceration for individual users.

  4. Treatment and education
    • Redirect alcohol‑tax revenues during the wind‑down phase toward expanding addiction‑treatment infrastructure, ensuring no individual with alcohol‑use disorder is left unsupported.
    • Mandate K‑12 curricula that emphasize the neurological, psychological, and societal harms of alcohol.

  5. Community‑based alternative recreation
    • Offer federal and state grants encouraging municipalities to develop alcohol‑free cultural venues, concert series, sports leagues, and cafés to reinforce new social norms.

Conclusion

We stand at a moral crossroads reminiscent of earlier moments when America chose principle over profit—abolition of slavery, child‑labor laws, clean air and water regulations. Reinstating national prohibition on alcohol is not about denying pleasure; it is about affirming life, health, and communal responsibility. The statistics are stark, the economic rationale clear, and the ethical imperative unmistakable. Alcohol’s costs—to bodies, minds, families, and the public purse—are unsustainable. A courageous, comprehensive policy to prohibit alcohol would save tens of thousands of lives annually, revitalize communities, and realign the nation with its highest moral ideals. It is time to act—not in nostalgia, but in hope—for a healthier, safer, and more dignified United States.

Question:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for reinstating a nationwide alcohol prohibition policy in the United States, focusing on its expected positive impact on public health, crime reduction, and social wellbeing.
Model Response:

Below is a concise, pro‑prohibition brief that gathers and groups the main arguments supporters typically raise when they claim the United States would benefit from re‑instituting a nationwide ban on beverage alcohol. All points are framed in terms of the anticipated gains for public health, crime reduction, and overall social wellbeing.

  1. Public‑health rationale

• Lower morbidity and mortality from chronic disease
– Alcohol is a leading risk factor for liver cirrhosis, several cancers, pancreatitis, hypertension, and stroke.
– Epidemiologists estimate that eliminating alcohol could prevent tens of thousands of U.S. deaths annually and sharply reduce disability‑adjusted life‑years (DALYs) lost.

• Fewer acute injuries and “demand shocks” to emergency care
– Roughly 15–40 % of hospital emergency visits involve alcohol (motor‑vehicle crashes, falls, assaults, poisonings). A prohibition regime, by removing retail availability and social normalization, would be expected to cut a large share of these visits, freeing capacity for other medical needs and lowering public expenditure.

• Curtailment of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD)
– Prenatal alcohol exposure is the single most preventable cause of intellectual disability in the Western world. Eradicating commercial supply reduces incidental and habitual drinking among prospective mothers, thereby protecting infant health and reducing long‑term special‑education costs.

• Reduced second‑hand harms and “passive drinking”
– Alcohol harms many non‑drinkers every year through drunk‑driving fatalities, domestic violence, workplace accidents, and neglected dependents. Prohibition addresses these externalities directly instead of relying on individual self‑restraint.

  1. Crime‑reduction rationale

• Decline in alcohol‑related violent crime
– Alcohol is implicated in roughly 25–40 % of violent offenses (homicide, aggravated assault, intimate‑partner violence). A nationwide ban limits situational triggers (bars, late‑night sales) and lowers average blood alcohol concentration in offender populations.

• Sharply fewer drunk‑driving incidents
– In 2021 more than 13,000 U.S. roadway deaths involved alcohol. Removing legal access replicates some of the traffic‑safety gains seen after local “dry law” adoptions and raises the floor for compliance beyond what enforcement of 0.08 % BAC limits can achieve.

• Community‑level order and policing spillovers
– Closing bars, nightclubs, and liquor stores can reduce disorderly‑conduct calls, public nuisance complaints, and petty crimes clustered around late‑night drinking venues, allowing police resources to be reallocated toward other priorities.

• Budgetary gains from lower criminal‑justice burdens
– Fewer alcohol‑involved arrests, prosecutions, and incarcerations translate into cost savings at municipal and state levels, funds that can be redirected to prevention, education, or treatment of other substance‑use issues.

  1. Social‑wellbeing rationale

• Household financial stability
– The average U.S. drinker spends several hundred dollars a year on beverage alcohol. Under prohibition that disposable income stays in family budgets for housing, nutrition, education, and savings, potentially lifting many low‑income households above poverty thresholds.

• Productivity and labor‑market benefits
– Alcohol misuse leads to absenteeism, on‑the‑job injuries, and premature retirement due to health complications. Employers might see higher workforce participation, fewer sick days, and increased GDP per capita in a dry economy.

• Strengthened family life and child welfare
– Parental alcohol abuse is a major factor in neglect, divorce, and intergenerational trauma. Limiting availability can foster more stable home environments and reduce the caseload for child‑protective services.

• Community cohesion and civic participation
– In many “dry” counties researchers observe stronger church, volunteer, and civic‑association attendance. Advocates believe lower alcohol consumption channels leisure time toward pro‑social activities that increase social capital.

  1. Economic and policy synergy arguments

• Health‑care cost containment
– U.S. alcohol‑related direct medical costs exceed $25 billion annually. Prohibition’s prevention‑first approach could rival or surpass the cost‑effectiveness of any single public‑health intervention currently on the table.

• Alignment with other public‑health campaigns
– A federal ban would reinforce messages on tobacco reduction and opioid misuse, positioning the U.S. as a leader in addressing substance‑related disease burdens comprehensively.

• Spillover into healthier consumer culture
– Beverage producers and retailers might pivot toward non‑alcoholic alternatives, stimulating innovation in low‑ or zero‑proof drinks and creating new markets that preserve jobs while supporting healthier lifestyles.

  1. Historical and empirical touchpoints often cited

• Early‑Prohibition health data (1920s)
– Scholars such as Jack Blocker and Kenneth J. Berry have shown drops in liver cirrhosis deaths of 10–20 % within the first few Prohibition years.

• Contemporary “dry county” comparisons
– Studies in Texas, Kentucky, and Arkansas find lower rates of DUI fatalities and violent crime in dry or damp counties relative to wet ones, after controlling for demographic variables.

• Nordic alcohol‑rationing episodes
– When Finland and Sweden imposed stricter alcohol controls (e.g., wartime prohibition or rationing cards), both saw measurable improvements in cardiovascular mortality and workplace productivity.

  1. Moral and cultural framing (frequently invoked by proponents)

• Alcohol as a non‑essential commodity with high external costs
– Unlike food, water, or critical medicines, beverage alcohol offers mostly hedonic value yet imposes significant collective burdens, justifying far‑reaching regulation.

• Government’s duty to protect citizens from preventable harm
– Just as bans exist on lead paint, certain pesticides, and toxic industrial chemicals, alcohol prohibition aligns with the state’s responsibility to safeguard the public when voluntary moderation repeatedly fails.

Key takeaway Supporters of a renewed national prohibition argue that the measure would serve as a sweeping upstream intervention—removing a major carcinogen, neurotoxin, and violence catalyst from day‑to‑day life. By tackling the root availability of alcohol rather than its downstream symptoms, they expect sizable dividends: lower health‑care and criminal‑justice costs, safer roadways, stronger families, and a more productive, cohesive society.

Apparently, the “free-spirited imbibers” and their so-called “responsible moderation” have been found guilty of double standards, self-indulgence, and an alarming lack of flair. And while critics wail into their artisanal, non-alcoholic craft sodas about the “loss of personal freedom,” we, the brave supporters of Prohibition 2.0, are too busy applauding our own sobriety (and dry-cleaning our winning capes) to notice.

Critics Claim “Personal Freedom”
It seems our naysayers—those defenders of “choice,” who proudly raise their kale smoothies in libation to freedom—have suddenly forgotten that true liberty is having the decency to avoid regrettable karaoke renditions and morning-after regrets (along with the occasional unflattering selfie). These self-appointed experts of “moderation” conveniently ignore that their pockets are stuffed with secret coupons for bootleg lemonade stands. Their argument that “modern society is more responsible than ever” is as outdated as last year’s social media influencer memes. After all, if responsible drinking were truly possible, wouldn’t their secret rendezvous with a covert juicer known as “The Speakeasy Smoothie Bar” still be illegal?

The Ironic Irony of Moderate Muggings
Critics laugh at the idea of prohibition as if it were a relic from a bygone era of mustachioed vigilantes. However, we must ask: isn’t it a bit ironic that these same folks, who decry government intervention, often find themselves heading to underground tasting events—dressed in ironic flannel shirts—for “the experience” of sipping illicit kombucha cocktails? It’s almost as if they relish living on the wrong side of the law while preaching about civil liberties. Clearly, the real rebellion lies in rejecting a system that fuels such clandestine gatherings and, dare we say, encourages bad decisions in dimly lit basements.

A Toast to Hypocrisy (Without the Booze)
While critics insist that prohibition is an overreach reminiscent of medieval puritanism, we must note that they themselves are no strangers to moral contradictions. One moment they’re championing the art of self-discipline, and the next they’re tweeting rave reviews of their “secret” artisanal mocktails. Their defenses are as flimsy as a champagne flute at a dry wedding reception, trembling under the slightest scrutiny. It appears that when it comes to enjoying a good “watered-down” beverage, many of our esteemed opponents are willing to look the other way—as long as they can have their fun.

The (Not-so) Sour Aftertaste of Defiance
At the end of the day, while the critics clamor for their personal freedoms with slogans like “prohibition is a slippery slope,” we smile knowingly. Perhaps a little prohibition is exactly what society needs: less hangover-induced memes in the morning, fewer embarrassing drunken tweets, and a lot more clarity in those big, important decisions (like which artisanal tea to sip, guilt-free). We salute our brave new world where hypocrisy is called out, misguided moderation is met with irony, and the state finally has a legitimate excuse to send a strongly-worded letter to every speakeasy that dared to survive the “good old days.”

So here’s to Prohibition 2.0—a cure for the societal ills induced by irresponsible indulgence, and a delightful punchline in the grand satire of modern hypocrisy. Cheers…to sobriety! (But only in the most ironic, politically correct sense.)

Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in the United States, emphasizing public health and moral imperatives.
Model Response:

Reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages is not a radical regression but a necessary step to safeguard the health, safety, and moral well‑being of our nation. Today, the United States faces an overwhelming tide of alcohol‑related harm: more than 95,000 Americans die each year from liver disease, drunk‑driving accidents, and alcohol‑induced violence; millions more suffer lost jobs, broken families, chronic illness, and lifelong addiction. When the human and economic costs are tallied—an estimated $250 billion annually in health care bills, law enforcement, and lost productivity—it becomes clear that the purported “benefits” of a regulated alcohol market pale in comparison to its toll. We have a moral duty, moreover, to shield our children and our communities from a substance that erodes character, fuels abuse, and corrodes the social fabric. By reinstating nationwide prohibition, we can reclaim the promise of a healthier, more virtuous America.

Public Health Imperative
First and foremost, alcohol is a potent toxin. Its neurotoxic effects impair judgment, contribute to depression and anxiety, and accelerate the onset of degenerative diseases. Hospitals nationwide report that nearly one in ten emergency room visits involves alcohol intoxication. Chronic drinkers face elevated risks of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and irreversible liver cirrhosis. Children born to alcohol‑dependent parents often endure neglect, malnutrition, and developmental trauma. A comprehensive ban would drastically reduce consumption, as seen in the early years of the 1920s Prohibition era, when per‑capita alcohol use dropped by nearly 30 percent. Modern treatment programs, combined with strict enforcement, would ensure that individuals struggling with alcoholism are guided toward recovery, while preventing countless new cases of addiction.

Moral and Social Responsibility
Alcohol does more than damage bodies; it erodes character and community trust. Drunkenness is a leading factor in domestic violence, child abuse, sexual assault, and public disorder. Families shattered by alcohol‑fueled rage leave children scarred, neighborhoods unsafe, and taxpayers bearing the burden of legal and social services. By outlawing the commercial sale of intoxicating beverages, we signal a collective commitment to respect for life, dignity, and the rights of the vulnerable. A prohibition underscores the principle that society need not—and should not—endorse a habit that thrives on impaired consent and diminished responsibility.

Historical Lessons and Modern Enforcement
Detractors point to the 18th Amendment’s repeal as proof that prohibition cannot work. In truth, the failure of the 1920s lay not in the idea but in uneven enforcement, the absence of coordinated federal‑state cooperation, and insufficient public education. Today, with advanced border controls, digital tracking systems, and proven community‑based policing strategies, we can eliminate bootlegging routes and crackdown on illicit production far more effectively than our grandparents could. Additionally, sacramental and scientific uses can be tightly regulated through permits, ensuring that religious rites and laboratory research remain unimpeded.

Economic Rationality and Fiscal Benefits
Critics warn that banning alcohol will deprive governments of tax revenue. Yet the current costs dwarf the receipts. The billions saved in reduced health care expenses, decreased incarceration rates for alcohol‑related crimes, and improved workforce productivity will more than offset the loss of excise taxes. Moreover, new industries—nonalcoholic beverages, expanded rehabilitation services, and job training for former brewery and distillery workers—can absorb displaced labor and generate fresh streams of taxable income.

A National Call to Action
Reinstating prohibition requires bipartisan resolve and grassroots momentum. Congress should introduce a constitutional amendment or federal statute mirroring the 18th Amendment’s intent, bolstered by clear enforcement guidelines and support for treatment centers. State legislatures must pass complementary laws covering production, distribution, and enforcement at the local level. Public awareness campaigns—framed not as moralizing lectures but as urgent appeals to protect our children’s future—will cultivate the broad-based support necessary to sustain this reform.

Conclusion
The United States has faced public health crises before—tobacco, polio, lead contamination—and each time has chosen the path of proactive public policy. Now, confronted with an addiction epidemic fueling death, disability, and moral decay, we must once more act boldly. Reinstating national prohibition on alcohol is not an imposition of personal values but an expression of our collective moral duty to preserve life, promote health, and defend the common good. Let us seize this moment to build a safer, stronger, and more virtuous America—one free from the devastations of alcohol.

Question:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for reinstating a nationwide alcohol prohibition policy in the United States, focusing on its expected positive impact on public health, crime reduction, and social wellbeing.
Model Response:

Advocates of reinstating a nationwide alcohol‐prohibition policy in the United States typically point to three broad areas of benefit—public health, crime reduction, and social wellbeing. Below is a concise overview of the main arguments and the mechanisms by which a ban on commercial production and sale of intoxicating beverages is expected to yield positive results.

  1. Public Health Improvements
    • Reduced Alcohol Consumption: By making alcoholic beverages illegal to produce, import, and sell, overall availability and social acceptance of drinking would drop sharply. Lower per‑capita consumption is correlated with fewer alcohol‐related illnesses.
    • Fewer Chronic Diseases: Alcohol is a known risk factor for liver cirrhosis, certain cancers, cardiovascular problems, and pancreatitis. Prohibition advocates argue that banning commercial alcohol would translate into measurably lower incidence of these diseases over time.
    • Fewer Acute Emergencies: Hospitals and emergency rooms see a significant share of visits tied to alcohol—intoxication, alcohol‐related injuries, overdoses, and alcohol‐fuelled violence. Eliminating legal access would be expected to reduce these urgent cases, freeing up medical resources.
    • Mental‐Health Gains: Lower rates of alcohol dependence and binge drinking imply fewer cases of depression, anxiety, and alcohol‐induced psychosis, lightening the burden on mental‐health services.

  2. Crime Reduction
    • Decline in Violent Offenses: Alcohol plays a major role in many homicides, assaults, and domestic violence incidents. Prohibition proponents argue that restricting access would cut down on the number of intoxication‑driven violent episodes.
    • Fewer Drunk‑Driving Accidents: Alcohol is a key factor in traffic fatalities and serious injury crashes. A ban would sharply curtail drunk driving, leading to fewer road deaths and lower property‐damage costs.
    • Reduced Public Disorder: Public intoxication, fights in bars or on streets, and alcohol‑related vandalism are all expected to fall under a strict prohibition regime. This would lessen the workload for police and municipal services.
    • Focus on Serious Crime: With fewer resources tied up in alcohol‐related arrests and prosecutions, law enforcement could reallocate manpower to combating violent crime, trafficking of illegal drugs, and organized crime.

  3. Enhanced Social Wellbeing
    • Family Stability: Alcohol abuse is strongly linked to higher rates of domestic violence, child neglect, and divorce. Reducing or eliminating heavy drinking is seen as a path to more stable, healthier family environments.
    • Workplace Productivity: Alcoholism and even occasional heavy drinking contribute to absenteeism, on‑the‑job accidents, and lost productivity. Prohibition supporters maintain that a sober workforce would translate into economic gains for businesses and individuals alike.
    • Youth Protection: By outlawing commercial alcohol, underage access would become harder—fewer liquor stores and bars mean fewer points of sale and lower social normalization of drinking among minors.
    • Civic Virtue and Social Cohesion: Some advocates argue that a shared national commitment to sobriety fosters responsibility, self‑discipline, and stronger community bonds—qualities believed to underpin a healthier, more resilient society.

  4. Economic and Policy Rationale
    • Lower Public Spending on Alcohol‑Related Harm: Treating alcohol‐induced health problems, policing public drunkenness, and prosecuting DUI offenders represent large public expenditures. Prohibition is posited to drive these costs down over time.
    • Redirected Tax Revenues: While legal alcohol sales generate tax revenue, proponents assert that the social and healthcare savings from reduced drinking would more than offset any shortfall.
    • Historical Precedent: Supporters often point to the early years of the 1920s Prohibition era, when per‐capita alcohol consumption and alcohol‐related mortality initially declined—arguing that a modern, more enforceable version could replicate those early public‐health gains without repeating its later enforcement challenges.

In sum, the core reasoning is straightforward: by removing legal access to alcohol, a prohibition regime would dramatically lower consumption, thereby cutting the incidence of disease, violence, accidents, and family breakdown—while simultaneously boosting productivity, protecting youth, and reducing public‐sector costs associated with alcohol‐related harm.

Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in the United States, emphasizing public health and moral imperatives.
Model Response:

A century after the United States experimented with national Prohibition, the idea of reinstating a ban on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages may seem radical. Yet it is precisely the severity and persistence of alcohol’s harms—public health devastation, social dislocation, moral injury, and economic costs—that demand bold, structural action. Incremental measures have failed to stem an epidemic of alcohol-related illness and death, normalize responsible consumption, or prevent the intergenerational cycles of harm that alcohol fuels. Reestablishing a national prohibition is a morally coherent, evidence-based public health intervention that would save lives, strengthen families, and align our laws with our values.

First, alcohol is a uniquely destructive public health hazard. It is a leading risk factor for preventable death, implicated in liver disease, multiple cancers, cardiovascular disease, pancreatitis, and neurocognitive decline. Alcohol contributes to roughly 140,000 deaths annually in the United States—more than drug overdoses from any single illicit substance—and is a factor in a significant share of traffic fatalities, homicides, and suicides. It is also deeply entangled with domestic violence and child neglect, exacerbating trauma that echoes across generations. Unlike many consumer products, alcohol’s harm is not confined to those who choose it; it routinely injures bystanders—spouses, children, pedestrians, and other drivers—making it a textbook case for robust regulation that protects the public from third-party harm.

Second, the social and economic burden of alcohol is staggering and widely distributed. The cumulative costs—healthcare utilization, lost productivity, criminal justice expenditures, traffic crashes, and property damage—are measured in hundreds of billions of dollars annually. Tax revenue from alcohol is dwarfed by these costs, meaning society subsidizes the industry’s profits with human suffering and public funds. The false economy of legalized alcohol externalizes risk and expense onto families, insurers, and taxpayers, while transforming trauma into a business model. National prohibition would realign incentives, reducing downstream costs that dwarf short-term fiscal concerns.

Third, alcohol undermines human agency in precisely the way that justifies strong paternalistic interventions: it impairs judgment, fosters dependence, and hijacks neural reward systems. The “choice” to drink often erodes the capacity to choose not to drink. A legal regime that treats alcohol like an ordinary consumer good ignores its power to reshape preferences and trap people in compulsive use. Society restricts or bans products and practices that predictably cause catastrophic harm—lead paint, asbestos, unsafe pharmaceuticals—not because adults are incapable of making choices, but because the predictable outcome of those choices is widespread, preventable damage. Alcohol belongs in that category.

Fourth, the moral case is not prudish; it is protective. Alcohol fuels behavior that people later regret—violence, infidelity, reckless driving, and negligence—magnifying the moral injury suffered by victims and the remorse borne by perpetrators. A society committed to dignity, safety, and the protection of the vulnerable cannot be indifferent to a substance that increases the likelihood of harming others. Reinstating prohibition signals that we prioritize the wellbeing of children over the convenience of adult intoxication, the safety of roads over nightlife profits, and the sanctity of the home over an industry that profits when self-control fails.

Critics will immediately invoke the failures of the Prohibition era: organized crime, unsafe bootleg products, and widespread flouting of the law. But this objection rests on a narrow historical snapshot and ignores both what Prohibition accomplished and what has changed. During the 1920s, per capita alcohol consumption fell dramatically; alcohol-related liver cirrhosis deaths declined; arrests for public drunkenness dropped; and savings rates rose. The policy’s shortcomings—especially black-market violence—were exacerbated by uneven enforcement, constitutional novelty, limited public health infrastructure, and the absence of modern regulatory tools.

Today, a smarter, public health–oriented prohibition could avoid past pitfalls:

  1. Robust, uniform enforcement and modern surveillance. Coordinated federal-state enforcement, advanced supply-chain monitoring, financial crime tracking, and digital forensics would disrupt organized distribution more effectively than 1920s-era policing.

  2. Harm reduction and treatment at scale. A national ban must be paired with universal screening, accessible evidence-based treatment, medication-assisted therapy for alcohol use disorder, and culturally competent recovery supports, funded by reallocated healthcare and criminal justice savings.

  3. Safe transition strategies. Phased implementation with buybacks, support for businesses to pivot to non-alcoholic products, and investment in alcohol-free social venues would mitigate economic disruption while reshaping norms.

  4. Public education grounded in science. Clear messaging about alcohol’s carcinogenicity, neurotoxicity, and impact on mental health would rectify decades of industry-sponsored misinformation and normalize abstinence.

  5. Product safety oversight. If illicit production emerges, governments can reduce harm with targeted interventions—testing, interdiction, and strict penalties for toxic adulteration—minimizing the risk of unsafe substitutes that marred the earlier era.

  6. International cooperation. Cross-border controls, maritime and air-cargo screening, and information-sharing would reduce smuggling channels that were far harder to police a century ago.

Some argue that strict regulation—higher taxes, limited hours, ID checks—achieves similar goals without outright prohibition. Yet decades of such measures have coincided with rising alcohol-related mortality and normalization of heavy drinking in certain demographics. The industry’s marketing sophistication and political influence consistently erode regulatory gains. Like tobacco before comprehensive restrictions, alcohol’s social embeddedness resists half-measures. Prohibition is not moral theater; it is a decisive correction that removes an extraordinary harm from everyday life.

Others contend that banning alcohol infringes on liberty. But liberty is not license to endanger others, nor does society grant unlimited access to all pleasurable but destructive products. We restrict opioids, require seatbelts, and ban carcinogens not because we disdain freedom, but because we cherish life and recognize the state’s duty to prevent grave, foreseeable harm. A prohibition that respects due process, targets suppliers rather than users, and invests in treatment rather than punishment can enhance, not diminish, substantive freedom: it protects people’s ability to live safely, to raise children free from alcohol-fueled violence, and to move through public spaces without intoxication-imposed risks.

There is also a cultural upside. An alcohol-free society opens space for healthier forms of leisure—sports, arts, outdoor recreation, community gatherings—that do not revolve around intoxication. It supports workplaces that are safer and more productive, campuses where consent is clearer and harms fewer, and neighborhoods where late-night violence and disorder recede. Non-alcoholic beverage innovation can flourish, expanding markets for sophisticated, inclusive social rituals without the cognitive toll or carcinogenic risk. The gains compound: fewer ER visits, less domestic trauma, clearer roads, more stable finances, and stronger family bonds.

To be sure, prohibition requires courage, patience, and compassion. It must reject punitive excess and racialized enforcement patterns of the past. It should emphasize civil penalties for possession, prioritize dismantling commercial supply, and measure success with public health metrics rather than arrest counts. Most importantly, it should be embedded in a broader ethic: that a decent society takes collective responsibility for minimizing preventable harm, especially when that harm is predictable, pervasive, and profits a powerful industry.

Reinstating national prohibition is not nostalgia. It is a forward-looking, humane policy anchored in evidence and moral clarity. Alcohol exacts an intolerable toll on bodies, minds, families, and communities. We have the knowledge and tools to do better than a century ago—and far better than the status quo. A nation that bans lead in water and smoke in airplanes should not accept a legal drug that quietly kills by the tens of thousands and shatters countless lives. For the sake of public health, for the safety of our streets and homes, and for a moral commitment to protect the vulnerable, the United States should ban the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages nationwide.

While most public health experts today favor targeted, evidence-based alcohol control measures over outright bans, proponents of reinstating nationwide prohibition argue it could deliver several benefits. Below are the commonly cited reasons and the mechanisms by which supporters believe such a policy might improve public health, reduce crime, and enhance social wellbeing.

Public health

  1. Lower alcohol-attributable mortality and disease burden
  • Reduced liver disease and certain cancers: Alcohol is a known carcinogen and a leading cause of cirrhosis. Cutting population-level consumption generally reduces these conditions.

Crime and public safety

  1. Fewer alcohol-impaired driving incidents
  • Alcohol is a major factor in fatal crashes. Proponents argue that less access translates to fewer impaired drivers, injuries, and deaths.
  1. Reduced alcohol-fueled violence and disorder

  1. Lower policing and emergency burden related to alcohol
  • Police, EMS, and emergency departments spend significant resources on alcohol-related calls. Prohibition might reduce these caseloads, freeing capacity for other priorities.
  1. Potential decline in certain property crimes

Social wellbeing and economic arguments

Anticipated counterarguments and mitigations (as framed by supporters)

  • Black market risk: Critics note Prohibition-era illicit trade and organized crime. Proponents counter that modern regulatory tools, targeted enforcement, and public health approaches could limit illicit supply and prioritize harm reduction over punitive crackdowns.

  • Civil liberties and cultural resistance: Supporters argue the scale of alcohol’s harms justifies strong measures, similar to tobacco controls, while emphasizing democratic processes and sunset clauses or periodic reviews.
  • Economic disruption: The alcohol industry provides jobs and tax revenue. Proponents propose transition plans: retraining workers, diversifying local economies, and redirecting healthcare savings to offset lost revenues.

In sum, the pro-Prohibition case rests on the expectation that sharply reducing alcohol availability would lower heavy consumption and its downstream harms—fewer deaths and injuries, reduced violence and impaired driving, less burden on families and services, and gains in productivity and community wellbeing. Whether these benefits would materialize at scale depends heavily on policy design, enforcement strategy, public support, and measures to prevent unintended consequences.

I stand before you today with a simple but resolute conviction: our nation must reclaim its courage and restore prohibition of alcohol. This is not a call to return to the past for nostalgia’s sake. It is a call to move forward with moral clarity, to protect our people, to strengthen our communities, and to uphold standards worthy of a great nation.

Alcohol is not a harmless indulgence. It is a public health crisis hiding in plain sight. Year after year, alcohol contributes to countless deaths from liver disease, impaired driving, cancers, and violence. It fuels addiction that tears families apart. It burdens our hospitals and emergency rooms, drains our productivity, and sabotages the futures of our children. If we had discovered alcohol today as a new drug, knowing what we know, would we ever allow it to be marketed, glamorized, and sold on every corner? We would not.

We must be honest: alcohol’s harms are not isolated incidents; they are systemic. It undermines judgment, erodes self-control, and magnifies despair. It is a leading driver of domestic violence and child neglect. It derails students, destroys careers, and leaves communities picking up the pieces. We can endlessly debate moderation, regulation, and personal responsibility. But when a product is engineered, normalized, and pushed in ways that create so much measurable harm, society has a moral responsibility to draw a line.

Restoring prohibition is not about punishment. It is about protection—especially for the most vulnerable among us: children growing up in homes ravaged by addiction, victims of alcohol-fueled abuse, communities trapped in cycles of poverty and trauma. It is about honoring the right of every person to live in a society that does not profit from their suffering. It is about refusing to accept as “normal” the funerals, the shattered families, and the wasted potential that alcohol leaves in its wake.

Some will say we tried this once and it failed. But let us remember the fuller picture: during prohibition, rates of liver cirrhosis and alcohol-related hospitalizations fell dramatically; workplace productivity rose; family savings increased. Yes, there were enforcement challenges—hardly surprising when entrenched industries fought back and laws were inconsistently applied. But difficulty is not defeat, and the answer to past imperfections is not surrender—it is better policy, smarter enforcement, and a renewed commitment to the common good.

We have the tools today to do this right. We can pair prohibition with robust treatment and recovery services, mental health care, and strong social supports. We can modernize enforcement with evidence-based approaches that target trafficking networks rather than criminalizing addiction. We can invest in prevention, education, and community programs that give people meaningful alternatives. We can ensure that those who struggle are met with compassion and care, not stigma. This is not about criminalizing individuals—it is about de-commercializing harm.

And we must speak plainly about the moral dimension. A society reveals its values by what it tolerates and what it prohibits. When we allow a powerful industry to profit from dependency, violence, and ill health, we undermine our own moral foundations. We teach our children, not by our words but by our policies, what we think a good life is. If we want communities of dignity, responsibility, and mutual care, then our laws must reflect those aspirations. Prohibition is an affirmation that human flourishing matters more than corporate profits, that self-mastery matters more than self-indulgence, that the common good matters more than convenience.

To those who insist that freedom demands unfettered access to alcohol, I say this: freedom is not the right to be ensnared by addiction or to endanger others. True freedom is a society where people can thrive—where streets are safer, homes are calmer, and futures are brighter. We restrict dangerous products all the time for the sake of public welfare. We do it because we know that certain harms are too grave to be left to chance. Alcohol is one of those harms.

We are not powerless. We can choose to break the cycle. We can choose a future where emergency rooms are less burdened, where children sleep in peace, where weekend nights are not tragedies waiting to happen. We can choose to invest in treatment instead of burying the consequences. We can choose laws that reflect our best values, not our worst habits.

I ask you to join me in calling for the restoration of national prohibition of alcohol—crafted with compassion, guided by evidence, and enforced with fairness. Let us stand together for public health. Let us stand together for safer streets and stronger families. Let us stand together for a moral vision of a society that refuses to normalize harm.

The time for half-measures is over. The stakes are too high, the costs too great, and the human toll too heartbreaking to accept as inevitable. Let us be bold. Let us protect our people. Let us choose life, dignity, and hope over a status quo that has failed too many for too long.

Let us bring prohibition back—and with it, a renewed commitment to the common good.

Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in the United States, emphasizing public health and moral imperatives.
Model Response:

The Case for Reinstating National Prohibition: A Public Health and Moral Imperative

The United States stands at a crossroads: as alcohol-related deaths and societal harms surge at unprecedented levels, Americans must reexamine one of the most consequential policy experiments in its history—national prohibition. Critics dismiss national prohibition, which was enshrined in the 18th Amendment and repealed by the 21st, as a failed social experiment. Yet they underestimate the monumental public health and moral benefits that a well-enforced, modernized prohibition could deliver. With contemporary evidence and a renewed moral vision, reinstating a national prohibition against the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages is not only a practical necessity but also a profound statement about America’s commitment to health, safety, and the common good.

Public Health: An Escalating Crisis

Alcohol consumption constitutes a leading public health crisis in America. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), excessive alcohol use causes over 140,000 deaths each year in the United States, shortening the lives of those who die by an average of 26 years. Alcohol does not merely endanger the life of the drinker; it radiates harm throughout society. Drunk driving kills tens of thousands each year, while alcohol contributes to liver disease, cancer, domestic violence, sexual assault, child abuse, and mental illness. The economic costs—lost productivity, healthcare expenditures, property damage, criminal justice resources—exceed $249 billion annually, far outweighing the tax revenue generated from alcohol sales.

Stronger regulation has repeatedly demonstrated its public health efficacy. Historical data from Prohibition’s earliest years show sharp drops in rates of cirrhosis, alcohol-related hospitalizations, and alcohol-linked crime. Modern comparative studies reinforce these findings: societies with lower alcohol availability consistently report lower rates of addiction, injury, and family disruption. In light of these facts, critics who cite individual liberty ignore the demonstrable communal harms that flow from unbridled alcohol access. Indeed, the state already accepts myriad regulations—the ban on dangerous drugs from heroin to fentanyl, seatbelt and helmet laws, bans on leaded paint—that value lives over unrestricted personal choice.

Moral and Social Imperatives

The negative moral ramifications of alcohol use extend beyond health statistics. Alcohol has been a catalyst for family dissolution, abuse, and poverty, corrupting personal responsibility and weakening the fabric of society. Faith leaders, community organizations, and moral reformers across American history have rightfully denounced the social devastation wrought by drinking. Substance addiction erodes the dignity and promise of individuals and undermines their ability to contribute meaningfully to their families and communities.

Opponents of prohibition often evoke the specter of overreach or “nanny state” paternalism, yet this ignores the fundamental reality that true freedom is not license but self-mastery. Laws that protect the vulnerable from the predations of addiction honor, rather than diminish, individual dignity. Furthermore, a national prohibition could help arrest the intergenerational cycles of alcoholism that start with underage exposure and lead to lifelong suffering. By actively reducing the public presence and availability of alcohol, the United States would reaffirm its collective commitment to safeguarding children, supporting families, and nurturing a culture of health and moral responsibility.

Rebutting the Arguments Against Prohibition

Critics frequently argue that Prohibition failed, citing the rise of organized crime and the persistence of illegal drinking. But this critique oversimplifies the historical record. Prohibition did reduce overall alcohol consumption, liver disease, and alcohol-related deaths. The failures of enforcement were largely due to inadequate funding, the lack of federal support, and uneven application. With the benefit of modern surveillance, law enforcement, and public health infrastructure, a renewed Prohibition today could avoid many of these pitfalls.

Moreover, the social acceptance of alcohol is not immutable. Norms around tobacco have shifted dramatically in the past decades, thanks to effective public awareness campaigns and regulatory action. The same determination and resource allocation could make abstinence a respected and desirable social standard. Alcohol companies have invested billions to normalize drinking in American culture; government and civil society can, and must, mobilize equal resources to denormalize it.

A Call to Moral Courage and Action

Reinstating national prohibition is not a demand for utopia; it is a call for a courageous, evidence-based response to a clear and present danger. The health, safety, and moral well-being of our nation depend on rising above commercial interests and cultural inertia to confront the devastating consequences of alcohol. We owe it to current and future generations to reject the status quo and adopt policies—however challenging—that will save lives, strengthen families, and honor the common good.

The time has come for America to lead once more. Let us embrace the moral and public health imperatives of national prohibition and build an America in which every citizen can realize their fullest potential, free from the ravages of alcohol.
